title: Milei, el capanga de Trump
content:
Para la Cancillería de Brasil, “Milei es un capanga de Trump”. La caracterización es harto justificada. Pero el dueño del chancho, Trump, quiere tomar por asalto a Brasil por medio de una injerencia militar contra el pretexto del “terrorismo”, o sea, una usurpación de la soberanía estatal de Brasil, así como por medio de una guerra comercial y sanciones financieras, la intromisión en el proceso electoral del país vecino y el apoyo sin restricciones a la ultraderecha y al fascismo brasileño. La histeria fascista de Milei, sobre todo, se encuentra motivada por la necesidad de que el Tesoro norteamericano salga, por tercera o cuarta vez, al rescate de las finanzas libertarias. El capanga argentino teme haber perdido el respaldo del Norte y tener que devaluar. Así como Donald Trump no consigue imponer sus exigencias en las guerras criminales en las que ha empeñado a Estados Unidos, Milei está llevando a Argentina a una bancarrota industrial y financiera, cuando comienza su cuarto año de gobierno. 

Por Política Obrera.







Para la Cancillería de Brasil, “Milei es un capanga de Trump”, según informa la prensa del país vecino. La caracterización es harto justificada. Pero el dueño del chancho, Trump, quiere tomar por asalto a Brasil por medio de una injerencia militar contra el pretexto del “terrorismo”, o sea, una usurpación de la soberanía estatal de Brasil, así como por medio de una guerra comercial y sanciones financieras, la intromisión en el proceso electoral del país vecino y el apoyo sin restricciones a la ultraderecha y al fascismo brasileño. El gobierno brasileño se ha visto obligado a negar la visa a tres funcionarios de Washington, que se habían arrogado la tarea de ‘supervisar’ a los organismos electorales de Brasil. Itamaraty, por otro lado, entiende que Lula es “un peso pesado de la política mundial”, que no debe cruzarse con “un peso pluma”. Pero si lo que importa, por cierto, no es el chancho sino quien le da de comer, el patrón de la estancia, Donald Trump, está empeñado en restablecer la hegemonía internacional del imperialismo norteamericano por medio de la guerra y, en especial, en su patio trasero. No cabe, entonces, rehuir una confrontación, sino desarrollarla en forma consecuente y apuntar a la cabeza mediante la movilización de masas.




Los sarcasmos de la diplomacia brasileña no constituyen una respuesta política a lo que es una ofensiva continental del imperialismo. Milei tiene agendado hacerse presente en la ceremonia de traspaso del mando presidencial a Keiko Fujimori, en Perú, y al de Adalberto de la Espriella, en Colombia, junto a toda la tropa fascista latinoamericana. Las reacciones diplomáticas de las cancillerías no alcanzan para derrotar esta ofensiva. Lula rehúsa apoyarse en una movilización popular debido a sus propios lazos con la burguesía local, que puebla el gabinete del Planalto. Esa movilización sólo partirá de una iniciativa independiente; el colombiano Gustavo Petro pagó caro su inmovilismo en cuanto a un llamado a la intervención de las masas.




Que Milei sea un capanga de Trump tiene otra implicancia, a saber, que Argentina ha caído al status de un protectorado de hecho. La coalición libertaria, compuesta por las fracciones internas de LLA, el PRO y numerosos gobernadores, no ha denunciado la provocación fascista de su candidato a la reelección. Tampoco ha habido un pronunciamiento ni tentativa de pronunciamiento en el Congreso; la agenda se establece en la Comisión de Labor Parlamentaria, que integran todos los partidos. Aunque no celebren los disparates del loco de atar, nadie tiene la intención de ponerle un chaleco de fuerza. El ‘flamante’ Jefe de Gabinete, Diego Santilli, aplaudió los insultos de Milei a Lula y a los miembros de la Suprema Corte de Brasil. El gobierno de Argentina se reduce a una banda de ‘hooligans’.




Pero la histeria fascista de Milei, sobre todo, se encuentra motivada por la necesidad de que el Tesoro norteamericano salga, por tercera o cuarta vez, al rescate de las finanzas libertarias. Para el FMI, sólo una devaluación del peso (a 1.800 por dólar, según el nuevo portavoz oficial) permitiría recaudar los dólares y los pesos para cubrir los vencimientos de deuda hasta finales de 2027. El FMI quiere divisas del saldo comercial para esos pagos y frenar la caída de la recaudación para conseguir los pesos; Luis Caputo quiere, por el contrario, que la cuenta la paguen mayores préstamos del FMI, el BID y el Banco Mundial, muy expuestos a la deuda pública de Argentina. El Tesoro de Argentina depende de socorros o swaps del Tesoro norteamericano y del Banco Central de China. Mientras que la línea de crédito de China financia el comercio de ese país con Argentina, los swaps del Tesoro norteamericano sólo sirven para financiar una salida de capitales.




El capanga argentino teme haber perdido el respaldo del Norte y tener que devaluar. Así como Donald Trump no consigue imponer sus exigencias en las guerras criminales en las que ha empeñado a Estados Unidos, Milei está llevando a Argentina a una bancarrota industrial y financiera, cuando comienza su cuarto año de gobierno.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: A new hunting season has been declared (pt. 2), or the normalisation of fascism
content:
On the 16th of July, at the invitation of Marco Rubio and the US State Department, representatives of over 60 countries 

gathered

 to hear Rubio 

annonce

 that “the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left”, wherever it might show itself, for “the left”, in its many incarnations, is the implacable enemy of the “West” and its civilization.










This is a distinctive and unique evil.  It has always been driven by a hatred above all else, a hatred for civilization itself.  It is a revolt of the worst against the best, a revolt of the weak and the cowardly against the strong and the good.  It is perpetrated by those who cannot build, who cannot create, who cannot achieve great things, and take their revenge upon the world for their own inadequacy by seeking to destroy those who can.  This is what radical leftism is.  It may wear various different slogans and ideologies across place and time.  They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist.  But the fundamental character is always the same.  It’s always the same. 




It is a poisonous resentment cloaked in the language of equality and justice and liberation, an overwhelming need to tear down what greater men have built, to wreck what is beautiful and what is right on behalf of people who are only filled with ugliness and have nothing else to offer the world.  Through violence and through terror, they once again seek to impose their ugliness on all of us.  The old dogma was wrong.  The old dogma was wrong; none of this is driven by idealism.  It is not utopian.  In fact, it is the opposite. 







If the threat comes from “within”, the “left” is nevertheless “transnational”, with financial and ideological support coming from countries such as Iran and 

Cuba

. (“Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory. … It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance. … Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.” –  from 

Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism

, published by the US state department, July 20, 2026. The report blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”) In other words, if the “indigenous left” of the USA is fundamentally a threat, it is ultimately a foreign, un-American threat which must be dealt with on a global scale through the construction of a new, “anti-leftist” global order.




After Rubio’s intervention, the stage was given to the White House deputy chief of staff, Steven Miller, whose 

words

 unveiled a much more radical vision.







It’s very important to understand that left-wing political terrorism seeks as its ultimate end the overthrow of our system and form of government. … 




Left-wing terrorism always ends in bloodshed, misery, and suffering.  It only can travel in one direction.  There’s no point at which the left-wing terrorist is satisfied with his gains and ceases progressing.  Inevitably, left to run its course, it always becomes a gulag.  It always becomes the mass imprisonment of political enemies, the stripping of their rights and freedoms, inflicting immense pain, humiliation, suffering in order to establish complete and total control – control through psychological and physical and actual terror.  And we have to understand that that is the scope and the extent of the threat that we face. 




As Secretary Rubio also pointed out, this is an international network.  Antifa, as an example, operates in dozens of countries all throughout the world.  They share common networks of funding and organization and information sharing.  And so, all of our intelligence agencies and law enforcement entities should be collaborating and coordinating and working together in order to root out these organizations. 




One of the hallmarks of left-wing violence and terrorism is its completely pretextual and disingenuous appeal to civil liberties in an effort to shield its own violence.  This is the tactic that the left always uses to try to protect itself from facing criminal punishment.  It is essential that we are wise enough and strong enough to understand that these appeals must fall on deaf ears.  When the leftist, who does not believe in freedom, who does not believe in civil rights, who does not believe in any ordered notion of justice, protests that we are violating his rights, understand that he is lying to try to persuade people who are not closely following the political scene that some injustice has been perpetrated against him. 




We must stay the course and be completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization.  If the left is allowed to use the real or actual threat of violence to destabilize our institutions, then those institutions cannot and will not succeed. …  




Nothing that we do works if the threat of violence and terror goes on unchecked.  Our political systems don’t work.  Our judicial systems don’t work.  Our legal systems don’t work.  Our jury trials don’t work.




At the same time, we have to understand there’s a real threat that those who are not themselves terrorists – but who support left-wing violence – will create the conditions that allow that violence to go on without any meaningful inhibition.  So, to be specific, we’ve seen some of our nation’s cities in America, like Washington, D.C. and New York City, something – again, it’s an American term, but it’s known as jury nullification.  This is when a person is obviously guilty of a crime but the juror, because they’re ideologically sympathetic to the perpetrator, will not sentence them to the crime which was obviously committed. 




We’ve seen in the United States, again and again, individuals who are part of left-wing organizations who’ve committed assaults against ICE officers or federal law enforcement, who’ve been brought to court, where clear evidence has been presented against them, that the jury has refused to convict for purely political reasons.  When you’ve reached that point, it demonstrates how deeply the cancer has begun to infest your society, where people have created an internal rationalization structure to justify unsanctioned violence against the state and state actors to achieve a political end. 




We have to use every lawful and legitimate tool that we have to demonstrate that justice will be served and delivered, and to prove that these kinds of tactics and techniques will ultimately fail.  If the leftist learns and observes that their violence and criminal activity helps and ultimately succeeds in achieving their desired political end, they will be endlessly emboldened. 




Here in the United States, we’ve seen a growing and deeply alarming increase in attempted assassinations against public figures, most notably, of course, the multiple assassination attempts against President Trump, the successful assassination attempt against Charlie Kirk, many others.  This is a fatal cancer to civilization.  And the greatest risk that we have is that our institutions have grown too soft and too cowardly to be able to defend themselves against a mortal threat. 




If your civilization is your home, you must defend it with the same passion and force as if an enemy intruder is inside your own house where your family lives.  That is the level of dedication and urgency that is required.  And the greatest threat is that even though there are far more of us, there are far more people who believe in order and civilization and liberty and the rule of law, is that if we are softer than those who seek to end us, then the smaller but more radical minority will succeed. 




It is easy to dismiss what I am saying and to say surely it cannot be that bad; it cannot be that dire.  But again, I point to the examples in our own country, where, for example, our Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which has been duly statutory authorized to carry out routine enforcements of immigration law, has been subjected to an over 8,000 increase – 8,000 percent increase in violent assaults.  These are not one-off episodes.  This is repeat, systemic, organized, funded insurrection, an armed resistance against the federal government.  There was a sniper from a sniper’s nest who, using an assault rifle, tried to shoot ICE officers in Dallas, Texas. 




These are the episodes that we’re talking about, where we have had repeated, direct, violent attacks on federal law enforcement in order to veto the ballot box with violence.  And the leftist justifies this violence to himself by saying that they alone are the arbiters of what is right or wrong – not the law, not history, not civilization, not public opinion, and certainly not God.  The leftist assumes for himself judge, jury, executioner. 




But let’s not pretend for a moment that these radical leftists, these terrorists, are operating from a place of sincere political conviction.  Sure, there are plenty of useful idiots that they use who may believe these discredited ideologies.  The leftist is fundamentally motivated by envy, by hatred, by jealousy.  The leftist looks at what is beautiful and what is good and what is natural and is filled with envy and hatred.  The leftist looks at a perfect family with a perfect life and a perfect job and perfect kids that goes to church every Sunday and is filled with a feeling of inadequacy and jealousy, and they covet.  And they turn those emotions ultimately into a desire to subjugate, to oppress, and to inflict pain and suffering.




It’s not a coincidence that when you look at these violent antifa demonstrations and you see any photograph of those who were assembled – to be blunt, not one of the people that is demonstrating looks like a normal person.  Not one looks normal.  They’re all deformed in some way – in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism.  Why is that?  Why?  If you look at two photographs and you see a normal American in the street and you see an Antifa protest, why do the people that are violently demonstrating – why is there not one normal-looking person among them?  Every one of them, through the course of their life and their decisions, has scarred their body and their appearance in many different ways, to the point in which their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred.




Trust your instincts to all people and across all civilizations.  You know what normal is.  You know what beautiful is.  You know what good is.  You know that families are right.  You know that children are precious and beautiful and must be protected.  You know that the criminal and the junkie and the predator is a threat to normal, healthy living.  This so much deeper than issues about taxation and regulation, although they’re incredibly important.  It’s about normal, healthy, ordered living. 




And the violent leftist, for these deep-seated reasons, going back to the earliest wisdom taught to us in the Bible about coveting – and I’m not talking about rich versus poor.  I’m talking about a much deeper kind of coveting – coveting people who are morally superior, who are superior in the simple, truthful way they live their lives, people that they look at who are happy and ordered and peaceful and contributing to their communities.  That burns an ember in them, and that’s how you end up with the horrors we’ve seen throughout history, where good families are dragged out into the street and executed. 







However much it might be of interest to analyse Miller’s phantasmatic paranoia, let us set aside the temptation to psychologise what he said and consider it a consequent political project. What Miller, Rubio and others of their kind object to on “the left” is not their purported violence – the violence unleashed by the Trump administration should be enough to convince anyone -, but the very idea of political equality and its place as a foundation stone for anything that can be called a 

democracy

.




We can argue about the virtues or vices of “democracy”, or about the different kinds of democracy, but anyone on the left – understanding by this term a broad, diverse and historical reality – would have to be mad to jettison the idea of it and its complex history altogether, and to not see that at the heart of the fascist project, among other things, is the denial of political equality and with it, any kind of democracy. To quote Umberto Eco and his essay, “

Ur-Fascism

“:







Elitism is a typical aspect of any reactionary ideology, insofar as it is fundamentally aristocratic, and aristocratic and militaristic elitism cruelly implies 

contempt for the weak

. Ur-Fascism can only advocate a 

popular elitism

. Every citizen belongs to the best people of the world, the members of the party are the best among the citizens, every citizen can (or ought to) become a member of the party. But there cannot be patricians without plebeians. In fact, the Leader, knowing that his power was not delegated to him democratically but was conquered by force, also knows that his force is based upon the weakness of the masses; they are so weak as to need and deserve a ruler. Since the group is hierarchically organized (according to a military model), every subordinate leader despises his own underlings, and each of them despises his inferiors. This reinforces the sense of mass elitism.







It is perhaps then not surprising that Donald Tump would close the day with a 

speech

 to the nation, informing everyone that the country’s election system is “so broken and so vulnerable that no one can possibly defend it. It is not defensible.” So much then for elections, for they are acceptable only when the election results correspond to the results desired and unacceptable – because undermined and corrupted by agents of foreign interests – when the outcome proves indigestable.




Again, quoting Eco: 







Ur-Fascism is based upon a 

selective populism

, a qualitative populism, one might say. In a democracy, the citizens have individual rights, but the citizens in their entirety have a political impact only from a quantitative point of view — one follows the decisions of the majority. For Ur-Fascism, however, individuals as individuals have no rights, and the People is conceived as a quality, a monolithic entity expressing the Common Will. Since no large quantity of human beings can have a common will, the Leader pretends to be their interpreter. Having lost their power of delegation, citizens do not act; they are only called on to play the role of the People. Thus the People is only a theatrical fiction. To have a good instance of qualitative populism we no longer need the Piazza Venezia in Rome or the Nuremberg Stadium. There is in our future a TV or Internet populism, in which the emotional response of a selected group of citizens can be presented and accepted as the Voice of the People. Because of its qualitative populism Ur-Fascism must be 

against “rotten” parliamentary governments

. One of the first sentences uttered by Mussolini in the Italian parliament was “I could have transformed this deaf and gloomy place into a bivouac for my maniples” — “maniples” being a subdivision of the traditional Roman legion. As a matter of fact, he immediately found better housing for his maniples, but a little later he liquidated the parliament. Wherever a politician casts doubt on the legitimacy of a parliament because it no longer represents the Voice of the People, we can smell Ur-Fascism.







Until then – until what remains of any semblance of democracy, or better yet, politics, is killed off – the US administration, under Trump’s orders and according to Stephan Miller, will “direct, for the first time in American history, all of our law enforcement and intelligence agencies to work together to disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest, and prosecute these political terrorists that are operating in our country.”







Suggested Reading (and the inspiration for this post):




Robert B. Shpiner, “Three speeches on a single day signaled a dying American democracy”, 

The Guardian

, 22/07/2026

author: Mosha Folger
title: Sanirajak man sentenced to four and a half years for sex crimes
content:
After a series of delays, Simeonie Issigaitok has received a four-and-a-half year sentence in a federal penitentiary for sexually touching children under the age of 16.

Court staff brought the 73-year-old Sanirajak man from into an Iqaluit courtroom Tuesday in a wheelchair. Through an interpreter, he listened expressionless, occasionally nodding his head, as Justice Christian Lyons read his sentence.

“Vulnerability of Inuit children and, in particular Inuit girls, is demonstrated by the persistent and troublingly high per capita rate of child sexual abuse in Nunavut,” Lyons said. “A problem that Mr. Issigaitok has repeatedly and substantially contributed to for decades.”

Issigaitok pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of sexual interference. The first offence occurred in Sanirajak sometime between 1987 and 1989. Issigaitok assaulted a girl in her early teens at her home while her parents were asleep.

The second incident occurred in April 2021. Issigaitok was captured on security video during a community event touching a boy while he was seated with a group of children.

On Tuesday, Lyons said aggravating factors included Issigaitok’s history of convictions for sex crimes dating back to  which dates back to 1988, his 2014 designation as a dangerous offender, and that his victims were Inuit children.

He also said that he considered the fact that Issigaitok attended residential school, where he was sexually abused, a mitigating factor, as well as Issigaitok’s guilty plea, which meant the victims did not have to testify.

Another mitigating factor was that one of the crimes occurred before the first of his 27 lifetime convictions. Therefore, the court could treat it as a first offense.

“This is attenuated somewhat by the fact that Mr. Issigaitok was abusing other children during the period of the offense and had committed a serious sexual assault a few years prior, for which he was sentenced in 1997,” Lyons said.

Crown prosecutors had sought a 10-year sentence, while defence lawyer Alan Regel argued that his sentence should be for time served in jail while his case worked its way through the legal system. Judges usually credit defendants with one and a half days for every day they spend in pre-trial custody. That means Regal was asking for a sentence of about 21 months.

Lyons sentenced Issigaitok to three years for the crime committed in 1988 and one and a half years for the crime committed in 2021.

Issigaitok will remain at the Aaqqigiarvik Correctional Healing Facility in Iqaluit while he awaits his transfer to a federal penitentiary to serve the two years and nine months left in his sentence.

The sentencing saw two delays. In June, Lyons delayed the proceeding to allow time for one victim to submit a statement. In July, Issigaitok was medevaced to Ottawa because of respiratory problems.

There was one more delay, of about an hour, on Tuesday. The scheduled court interpreter was not in town, and court staff needed to videoconference a new one.

author: Equality Now
title: Justice delayed across borders: What the Tate cases reveal about the cost of system failure
content:
For years, women have come forward with allegations of sexual violence against Andrew and Tristan Tate. Investigations have unfolded in Romania. Civil proceedings have taken place in the United Kingdom. Criminal charges now span multiple jurisdictions. Most recently, the brothers were jailed in the United States while awaiting extradition to the UK, where they will face charges including rape, trafficking for sexual exploitation, assault and other serious offences. They deny all allegations.

Taken together, these developments should represent a significant step toward accountability. Instead, they raise an unsettling question:

Why does it take allegations across multiple countries, years of investigations and extensive public evidence before justice systems begin to catch up?

The answer is linked to the numerous and persistent failures of the institutions responsible for delivering justice and protecting the most vulnerable from exploitation.

Accountability should not depend on crossing borders

The allegations against the Tate brothers, known for their social media presence , have involved conduct said to have occurred across different countries over many years, creating overlapping investigations spanning multiple jurisdictions, and resulting in lengthy legal processes.

Often in trafficking cases, survivors have to navigate different legal systems, evidentiary standards and repeated delays while proceedings unfold; the multiple cases involving the Tate brothers are no different.

In Romania, prosecutors allege that the brothers formed an organised criminal group that recruited and exploited women, including through methods of psychological pressure and control, and have charged them with human trafficking and rape.

In the United Kingdom, prosecutors have authorised charges including rape, actual bodily harm and arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Whether perpetrated across physical and digital spaces or across national borders, exploitation exists on a continuum , and justice systems should be equipped to respond accordingly and in a timely manner. Yet too often, laws, institutions and enforcement mechanisms remain siloed, creating gaps that traffickers and exploiters can exploit.

International human rights law already provides a framework for tackling these crimes. The Palermo Protocol defines trafficking as the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of persons through threats or use of force, coercion, abduction, deception, abuse of a position of vulnerability or other prohibited means for the purpose of exploitation and calls on States to work together to prevent trafficking, protect survivors, investigate offences and prosecute perpetrators.

The recent extradition proceedings in the Tate cases demonstrate that international cooperation is possible. But they also expose how long survivors may be forced to wait before justice systems work together effectively.

Understanding patterns of systematic exploitation

As outlined in this in-depth piece by The New Yorker, perhaps the most disturbing aspect of these cases involving the Tate brothers is the consistency of the alleged methods used to violate and traffic a number of individuals.

From allegations of calculated recruitment, coercive control, financial exploitation, to sexual violence, these alleged acts have been highlighted as patterns as part of an organised business model rather than isolated crimes.

Recognising these patterns is important to defining the crime as the human rights violation it is,  because trafficking rarely resembles the stereotypes many people still imagine.

Trafficking can take many forms and humans can be trafficked for many reasons. Survivors can be trafficked for sexual exploitation, forced labour, domestic servitude, or forced criminality, among other things. Often these forms of exploitation are interconnected, and many survivors have experienced multiple forms of exploitation once trafficked.

Under international human rights law, trafficking is defined by its exploitative purpose, and while people of all genders can experience trafficking, women and girls are disproportionately affected by trafficking for sexual exploitation.

When prosecutors in Romania accused Andrew and Tristan Tate of recruiting women through the “lover boy” method of building romantic or emotional relationships with women before allegedly using manipulation, coercion, and violence to exploit them for sexual content and financial gain, it becomes very clear that systems should be required to respond and prevent this form of harm from happening in the first place.

While the brothers deny all allegations, the crimes they are accused of are illustrative of how sex trafficking often operates through patterns of coercion and control rather than a single act of violence. Governments have obligations to prevent exploitation, protect survivors and ensure perpetrators are held accountable. Meeting those obligations requires justice systems that can identify patterns, investigate effectively and respond before harm takes place.

Misogyny is not separate from exploitation

The allegations against the Tate brothers cannot be separated from the ideology that helped build their influence. Misogyny is permeating our online spaces, our justice systems, and shaping the minds of young people.

As Jackson Katz recently argued , Andrew Tate is not merely an internet provocateur but a prominent figure within a broader anti-feminist movement that normalises women’s subordination while portraying gender equality as a threat. His public statements have repeatedly promoted ideas of male dominance, entitlement and control over women.

While these ideas do not in themselves prove misconduct or a crime, they reflect and reinforce broader cultural beliefs and attitudes that fuel the cultural apathy around gender equality and contribute to an environment that enables our justice systems to continue to repeatedly fail survivors.

It is time for us to question where accountability can be accessed when misogyny becomes profitable .

Delays in justice come at a cost

The latest extradition request by the United Kingdom offers hope that accountability may finally be within reach, but survivors may still face months, or even years, before the allegations are heard in a UK criminal court.

But justice systems need to keep pace.

Currently in jail in Miami, the brothers are challenging extradition at every stage. The UK has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the US State Department. Between hearings, appeals, and a decision by the Secretary of State, it is entirely plausible that extradition proceedings alone could take anywhere between 6–18 months.

Worldwide, survivors continue to face significant barriers when seeking justice, particularly where systems fail to identify manipulation, coercion and abuse of power as indicators of exploitation.

And every year that serious allegations remain unresolved, the risk of harm to survivors and loss of public trust in the justice system increases. Delays can discourage survivors from reporting, allow harmful narratives to flourish, and send a damaging message that power, wealth or online influence can be a pass for impunity to thrive.

We are hopeful that the Tate cases, instead of simply remaining another attention-grabbing headline in a long-running legal battle, will serve as an impetus for strengthening international cooperation, improving responses to trafficking and sexual violence, and ensuring that survivors are not left waiting years for justice because exploitation crossed a border.

contentBlocks.text: For years, women have come forward with allegations of sexual violence against Andrew and Tristan Tate. Investigations have unfolded in Romania. Civil proceedings have taken place in the United Kingdom. Criminal charges now span multiple jurisdictions. Most recently, the brothers were jailed in the United States while awaiting extradition to the UK, where they will face charges including rape, trafficking for sexual exploitation, assault and other serious offences. They deny all allegations.
Taken together, these developments should represent a significant step toward accountability. Instead, they raise an unsettling question:
Why does it take allegations across multiple countries, years of investigations and extensive public evidence before justice systems begin to catch up?
The answer is linked to the numerous and persistent failures of the institutions responsible for delivering justice and protecting the most vulnerable from exploitation.
Accountability should not depend on crossing borders

The allegations against the Tate brothers, known for their social media presence , have involved conduct said to have occurred across different countries over many years, creating overlapping investigations spanning multiple jurisdictions, and resulting in lengthy legal processes.

Often in trafficking cases, survivors have to navigate different legal systems, evidentiary standards and repeated delays while proceedings unfold; the multiple cases involving the Tate brothers are no different.

In Romania, prosecutors allege that the brothers formed an organised criminal group that recruited and exploited women, including through methods of psychological pressure and control, and have charged them with human trafficking and rape.
In the United Kingdom, prosecutors have authorised charges including rape, actual bodily harm and arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Whether perpetrated across physical and digital spaces or across national borders, exploitation exists on a continuum , and justice systems should be equipped to respond accordingly and in a timely manner. Yet too often, laws, institutions and enforcement mechanisms remain siloed, creating gaps that traffickers and exploiters can exploit.

International human rights law already provides a framework for tackling these crimes. The Palermo Protocol defines trafficking as the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of persons through threats or use of force, coercion, abduction, deception, abuse of a position of vulnerability or other prohibited means for the purpose of exploitation and calls on States to work together to prevent trafficking, protect survivors, investigate offences and prosecute perpetrators.

The recent extradition proceedings in the Tate cases demonstrate that international cooperation is possible. But they also expose how long survivors may be forced to wait before justice systems work together effectively.
Understanding patterns of systematic exploitation

As outlined in this in-depth piece by The New Yorker, perhaps the most disturbing aspect of these cases involving the Tate brothers is the consistency of the alleged methods used to violate and traffic a number of individuals.

From allegations of calculated recruitment, coercive control, financial exploitation, to sexual violence, these alleged acts have been highlighted as patterns as part of an organised business model rather than isolated crimes.
Recognising these patterns is important to defining the crime as the human rights violation it is,  because trafficking rarely resembles the stereotypes many people still imagine.

Trafficking can take many forms and humans can be trafficked for many reasons. Survivors can be trafficked for sexual exploitation, forced labour, domestic servitude, or forced criminality, among other things. Often these forms of exploitation are interconnected, and many survivors have experienced multiple forms of exploitation once trafficked.

Under international human rights law, trafficking is defined by its exploitative purpose, and while people of all genders can experience trafficking, women and girls are disproportionately affected by trafficking for sexual exploitation.

When prosecutors in Romania accused Andrew and Tristan Tate of recruiting women through the “lover boy” method of building romantic or emotional relationships with women before allegedly using manipulation, coercion, and violence to exploit them for sexual content and financial gain, it becomes very clear that systems should be required to respond and prevent this form of harm from happening in the first place.

While the brothers deny all allegations, the crimes they are accused of are illustrative of how sex trafficking often operates through patterns of coercion and control rather than a single act of violence. Governments have obligations to prevent exploitation, protect survivors and ensure perpetrators are held accountable. Meeting those obligations requires justice systems that can identify patterns, investigate effectively and respond before harm takes place.
Misogyny is not separate from exploitation

The allegations against the Tate brothers cannot be separated from the ideology that helped build their influence. Misogyny is permeating our online spaces, our justice systems, and shaping the minds of young people.

As Jackson Katz recently argued , Andrew Tate is not merely an internet provocateur but a prominent figure within a broader anti-feminist movement that normalises women’s subordination while portraying gender equality as a threat. His public statements have repeatedly promoted ideas of male dominance, entitlement and control over women.

While these ideas do not in themselves prove misconduct or a crime, they reflect and reinforce broader cultural beliefs and attitudes that fuel the cultural apathy around gender equality and contribute to an environment that enables our justice systems to continue to repeatedly fail survivors.
It is time for us to question where accountability can be accessed when misogyny becomes profitable .
Delays in justice come at a cost

The latest extradition request by the United Kingdom offers hope that accountability may finally be within reach, but survivors may still face months, or even years, before the allegations are heard in a UK criminal court.
But justice systems need to keep pace.

Currently in jail in Miami, the brothers are challenging extradition at every stage. The UK has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the US State Department. Between hearings, appeals, and a decision by the Secretary of State, it is entirely plausible that extradition proceedings alone could take anywhere between 6–18 months.
Worldwide, survivors continue to face significant barriers when seeking justice, particularly where systems fail to identify manipulation, coercion and abuse of power as indicators of exploitation.

And every year that serious allegations remain unresolved, the risk of harm to survivors and loss of public trust in the justice system increases. Delays can discourage survivors from reporting, allow harmful narratives to flourish, and send a damaging message that power, wealth or online influence can be a pass for impunity to thrive.

We are hopeful that the Tate cases, instead of simply remaining another attention-grabbing headline in a long-running legal battle, will serve as an impetus for strengthening international cooperation, improving responses to trafficking and sexual violence, and ensuring that survivors are not left waiting years for justice because exploitation crossed a border.

title: Selective Ritual Reform and Buddhist Marriage Among Ambedkarites in Odisha
content:
Abstract: Marriage rituals in South Asia have historically reinforced caste and gender hierarchies. Within contemporary Ambedkarite Buddhist communities in Odisha, debates over “mixed marriages” frequently centre on visible Hindu practices such as Brahmin priests, sindur , and the mangalsutra . Drawing on Ambedkarite social media discussions, wedding practices, B. R. Ambedkar’s writings, and anthropological studies of marriage, this article argues that such critiques are often selective. While many Ambedkarites reject Brahmanical symbols, they continue practices such as the baraat , engagement rituals such as Nadia Dhara ( ring ceremonies), status matching in partner selection, and competitive wedding display. These practices reproduce caste, gender, and status hierarchies in new forms. This article argues that Ambedkarite Buddhist marriage remains an evolving social project. Its transformative potential depends on changing the social relations that organise marriage, not simply replacing Brahmanical symbols. It calls on Dalit Bahujan communities to reimagine Buddhist marriage as an ethical practice grounded in equality, solidarity, and collective uplift.

Introduction: Hindu marriage has often been understood as a religious and soteriological event embedded within broader moral and ritual frameworks (Harman, 1987). At the same time, marriage has historically operated as a key social institution through which caste, gender, and hierarchy are regulated and reproduced (Ambedkar, 1916/1979). As Ambedkar argued, the endurance of caste rests significantly on the regulation of marriage, particularly through endogamy and the control of women’s mobility and sexuality. Rituals surrounding marriage are therefore not incidental cultural practices but central mechanisms through which social order is maintained, reproduced, and publicly displayed.

However, marriage also carries the potential for transformation, especially within communities committed to equality and social justice. In the context of Ambedkarite marriage, it becomes a critical site for practising dignity, equality, and mutual respect. At the same time, inherited caste and patriarchal structures can continue to persist in new forms within intimate relationships. It is within this tension between reproduction and transformation that the significance of marriage must be understood. For Ambedkar, challenging caste required transforming both political institutions and everyday social practices that maintain caste boundaries.

The mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956 formed part of this broader social project. Conversion signified a rejection of Brahmanical religious authority, and an embrace of an ethical framework based on equality and rationality (Ambedkar, 1957). Yet the question of how marriage is practised within Ambedkarite communities remains open.

In recent years, debates within Ambedkarite circles in Odisha have increasingly focused on what many describe as “mixed marriages.” The term refers to weddings that identify themselves as Buddhist while simultaneously incorporating rituals and practices associated with Hindu traditions. These include the presence of Brahmin priests, Sanskrit mantras, fire rituals, dowry exchanges, and engagement or practices such as kanyadaan and the symbolic “gift of the daughter.” In many marriages, families also continue to rely on astrology through kundali matching and the selection of an auspicious muhurat, practices that shape ideas of compatibility, timing, and ritual legitimacy. Ambedkarite activists and commentators often criticise these practices because they reproduce Brahmanical structures of caste, thereby weakening the emancipatory potential of Buddhist marriage. Such critiques frequently draw upon Ambedkar’s analysis of caste, endogamy, and the social regulation of marriage, and emphasise that ritual reform is central to the broader project of annihilating caste.

However, contemporary discussions also reveal an important asymmetry. While explicitly Hindu ritual elements are strongly criticised, other practices common within Ambedkarite weddings receive little scrutiny. One such practice is the baraat, the celebratory procession in which the groom travels to the bride’s home accompanied by music, dancing, and relatives. This article examines why certain rituals become objects of critique while others remain normalised within Ambedkarite communities in Odisha. I argue that critiques of “mixed marriage” tend to focus on visible and easily identifiable symbols rather than the deeper social structures embedded in ritual practice. As a result, while overtly Brahmanical elements are rejected, underlying patterns of caste and gender hierarchy often remain insufficiently examined.

This paper examines contemporary Ambedkarite debates on marriage in Odisha, focusing on caste, gender, Hindu marriage norms, and Ambedkarite alternatives. While marriage as a social institution requires further exploration, future research will examine its relationship with patriarchy, caste, gender, and social transformation across diverse communities and caste and religious traditions.

This article is structured as follows. This article begins with a methodological and positional note, followed by anthropological perspectives on marriage and Ambedkar’s understanding of caste and endogamy. It then examines the historical background of the baraat. Then it discusses contemporary Ambedkarite debates on ritual reform, gender, status matching, and wedding display. The final section argues that Ambedkarite marriage remains an evolving ethical and social project.

Methodological and Positional Note

This article adopts an interpretive and reflexive approach to contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices in Odisha, combining anthropological reflection with engagement in Ambedkarite social worlds. The analysis does not present a formal ethnographic field study based on structured interviews or systematic participant observation. The discussion draws on observations of Ambedkarite wedding ceremonies in parts of Odisha, as well as conversations and debates circulating on social media platforms and community networks, where questions surrounding “mixed marriages” are actively negotiated.

As a native of Odisha and an Ambedkarite observer, my engagement with these practices is both experiential and analytical. This positionality allows close attention to the everyday ways in which rituals are performed, interpreted, defended, and contested within the community. At the same time, the article does not claim neutrality or complete externality from the social world being analysed. In this sense, the paper is informed by a reflexive sociological orientation (Bourdieu & Wacquant, 1992), recognising that the social and intellectual worlds also shape the observer under examination. This approach also reflects a broader anthropological recognition that contemporary debates over ritual, morality, and identity are increasingly mediated through digital platforms and informal discussion networks. This article presents a theoretically informed interpretation of patterns that are socially visible, widely discussed, and culturally significant within Ambedkarite contexts in Odisha.

Observing Ambedkarite Public Discourse

Social media platforms, especially Facebook and Instagram, have become important arenas where Ambedkarites share wedding photographs, videos, and reflections. In these discussions, people often debate whether a ceremony was “properly Buddhist” or whether it included Hindu ritual elements. Criticism usually focuses on visible markers such as Brahmin priests, Sanskrit mantras, fire rituals, dowry, or kanyadaan . These elements are interpreted as signs that the ceremony remains shaped by Brahmanical traditions. Many Ambedkarites frequently invoke Ambedkar’s critique of caste and stress that Buddhist weddings should reflect anti-caste values.

Scholars of digital anthropology note that social media increasingly functions as a space where communities negotiate identity, morality, and cultural norms through everyday interaction (Miller et al., 2018). Alongside these digital observations, I also attended and closely observed a Buddhist wedding within an Ambedkarite community in Odisha. Conversations surrounding the ceremony reflected similar concerns about avoiding Hindu rituals and preserving Buddhist ethical principles. Yet the baraat procession remained one of the most celebrated and emotionally charged moments of the wedding. The groom’s arrival, music, dancing, and symbolic display generated collective excitement and pride. This article focuses on this tension: while some rituals are identified and criticised as Brahmanical, the baraat and other rituals continue to be normalised as culture, celebration, and Ambedkarite assertion. In many contemporary Ambedkarite weddings, the baraat has become a central spectacle of identity, prestige, and public performance.

The Historical Background of the Baraat

Classical Hindu texts reflect the patrilineal logic underlying many South Asian marriage systems. The Manusmriti , for example, places women under the authority of father, husband, and son, while kanyadaan symbolically transfers the bride into her husband’s lineage (Doniger & Smith, 1991). This text does not describe the contemporary baraat . Rather, they illustrate the broader social structure of patriliny and bride transfer that later marriage rituals came to express in different ways.

The contemporary baraat is a much later historical development. It became widely established during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries (c. 1800–2000), when wedding processions associated with royal and dominant-caste marriage practices spread across many caste communities through social mobility, colonial modernisation, and urbanisation. As the procession became more widely adopted, it came to publicly enact kinship alliance and patrilocal marriage. The groom travels with relatives, music, and celebration to the bride’s household, marking the alliance between families and the incorporation of the bride into the groom’s lineage (Selwyn, 1979). The procession also has historical connections to royal and martial culture. In premodern South Asia, horses symbolised sovereignty, masculine prestige, and warrior authority. Mounted processions, in which rulers and elite men rode on horseback during public ceremonies, were associated with kingship and high social status (Richards, 1978). Meadows (2013) similarly argues that horseback display functioned as a marker of embodied masculinity and social distinction. Over time, these elite forms of ceremonial display became incorporated into wedding rituals through the groom’s mounted procession.

Anthropological Perspectives on Marriage

Ambedkar’s early writings themselves constitute an important anthropological and ethnological analysis of caste, gender and marriage. In Castes in India , he argued that caste survives through endogamy and the regulation of marriage (Ambedkar, 1916/1979). Marriage rituals, therefore, are not politically neutral cultural practices but central mechanisms through which caste and gender hierarchy are reproduced and maintained.

Anthropological studies show that South Asian marriage is structured through unequal relations between wife-givers and wife-takers. Lévi-Strauss (1969) viewed marriage as a system of exchange that organises kinship alliances, while Selwyn (1979) argues that these rituals reproduce a social order in which honour and authority are associated with men, wife-takers, and higher-status groups, and women and wife-givers occupy subordinate positions.

Ethnographic research from Khalapur further found that Rajput weddings were procedurally “almost the same” as those of Brahmins and Dalit communities such as Chamars and Chuhras (Kolenda, 1984, p. 99). This suggests that hierarchical marriage forms are widely reproduced through social imitation and cultural continuity. From this perspective, the baraat is more than a celebration. It embodies masculine prestige, lineage, and caste hierarchy, yet it has rarely been questioned within contemporary Ambedkarite debates.

Baraat, Caste Prestige, and Dalit Exclusion

The baraat , particularly the groom riding a horse and sometimes carrying a sword, has long been associated with dominant-caste and warrior traditions in South Asia. For Dalits, however, such displays were historically restricted (Khandekar & Majumdar, 2026). In several parts of India, Dalit grooms have faced threats, humiliation, violence, and even murder for riding horses during wedding processions because the act was seen as a challenge to caste hierarchy. Contemporary incidents across North and Western India show that the mounted baraat remains a visible marker of dignity, status, and caste assertion (Khandekar & Majumdar, 2026). In this context, a Dalit or Ambedkarite groom riding a horse can represent a powerful assertion of dignity against historical exclusion. Yet this assertion does not automatically dismantle the hierarchical meanings embedded in the ritual. Does adopting the baraat represent liberation, or does it reproduce the social structures that anti-caste politics seeks to transform?

The political logic of the Kalaram Temple Entry Satyagraha, led by Ambedkar on 2 March 1930, offers an important way to think about this tension. Ambedkar’s entry into the temple did not affirm Hindu worship; it asserted equal rights and human dignity. Likewise, a Dalit groom riding a horse may challenge historical exclusion. However, this does not require preserving the baraat as a whole. Equality can be claimed without reproducing the caste hierarchy and patriarchal choreography through which the ritual historically acquired its meaning. Assertion, therefore, need not entail repetition.

Reimagining Buddhist Marriage: Between the Annihilation of Caste and Dhamma

If marriage reproduces caste, as Ambedkar argued (see ” Caste in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development”), then the question is how marriage should be reimagined within an Ambedkarite Buddhist framework. In The Buddha and His Dhamma , Ambedkar presents Buddhism not as a religion of ritual but as a moral and social philosophy grounded in liberty, equality, and fraternity. Rather than prescribing a fixed model of marriage, he offers ethical principles through which marriage can be rethought beyond caste hierarchy and patriarchal control. From this perspective, Buddhist marriage cannot simply mean replacing one set of rituals with another. It requires transforming the social relations through which caste and patriarchy are reproduced. Marriage must be grounded in equality, dignity, compassion, and shared responsibility rather than lineage, hierarchy, or control. The emphasis shifts from ritual performance to ethical relationships and everyday social practice.

This understanding also strengthens the critique of contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices. Rejecting visible Brahmanical symbols alone is not enough if marriage continues to reproduce hierarchy through everyday practices. The absence of a fixed Buddhist marriage model should therefore be understood not as a limitation but as an opportunity. It invites each generation to develop marriage practices that reflect the anti-caste vision of Annihilation of Caste and the ethical principles of The Buddha and His Dhamma . In this sense, Ambedkarite Buddhist marriage remains an evolving project of ethical and social transformation.

Selective Ritual Critique and the Persistence of the Baraat

Contemporary Ambedkarite debates on “mixed marriages” rarely question the baraat . Instead, criticism usually targets visible Hindu practices such as Brahmin priests, sindur , mangalsutra , or dowry. Yet these critiques are often selective. Many weddings appear Buddhist in form while continuing practices such as the baraat , kanyadaan , or large-scale economic expenditure. The issue, therefore, is how social relations and hierarchies continue to organise marriage.

Ambedkar (1916/1979) argued that caste reproduces itself through endogamy, imitation, and the habitual observance of inherited customs and social practices. Bourdieu’s concept of habitus (1977) further explains how these practices become internalised through everyday life until they appear natural and self-evident. Ethnographic observations from North India support this argument. Kolenda (1984, p. 99) found that Rajput weddings were procedurally “almost exactly the same” as those among Brahmins and Dalit communities such as Chamars and Chuhras, showing how ritual forms are reproduced across communities through social imitation and cultural continuity. This helps explain why the baraat remains largely unquestioned in many Ambedkarite weddings in Odisha. Its dominant-caste origins are often recognised, yet the ritual continues to be celebrated. Celebration, status, and emotional attachment make the procession difficult to question. The festive atmosphere obscures the unequal social relations embedded within the ritual, allowing caste and patriarchal relations to persist through everyday practice.

Selective critique also operates within Ambedkarite communities themselves. Individuals with greater symbolic authority often shape what counts as a “proper” Ambedkarite marriage. Yet similar inconsistencies appear across generations. Even some first- and second-generation educated Ambedkarites who strongly criticise Brahmanical rituals have themselves celebrated weddings with baraat processions, sindur , dowry, or lavish wedding expenditure. In some cases, they have publicly criticised or even refused to attend the weddings of fellow Ambedkarites, describing them as “Brahmanical,” while overlooking similar practices in their own marriages. This produces an uneven politics of ritual reform in which certain rituals become markers of ideological purity, while others remain protected by emotional attachment, patriarchal privilege, cultural familiarity, or symbolic prestige. This unevenness is also gendered. Rituals associated with women become the primary targets of ideological scrutiny, while male-centred practices such as the baraat remain largely unquestioned. Critique, therefore, reflects not only ideological disagreement but also unequal relations of gender, recognition, legitimacy, and symbolic power within the movement.

At the same time, these practices are not static. Many Ambedkarite weddings consciously reshape the baraat through new political symbols. Grooms carry portraits of Ambedkar, blue flags accompany the procession, and Ambedkarite songs replace conventional wedding music. These practices express Dalit dignity, assertion, and public visibility in a society that historically denied such recognition. Yet an important question remains. Does adding Ambedkarite symbols transform the social structure of the ritual, or does it place new political meanings onto an inherited ceremonial form? If the procession continues to centre masculine mobility, lineage assertion, and the asymmetrical incorporation of the bride into the groom’s family, then its underlying social logic may remain largely intact. The Ambedkarisation of the baraat therefore illustrates the continuing tension between symbolic assertion and structural transformation within contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices in Odisha.

Beyond Sindur and Mangalsutra : Gender and Ritual Reform

Within Ambedkarite discussions, sindur and mangalsutra are frequently criticised as visible symbols of Brahmanical patriarchy and women’s subordination. Many Ambedkarite Buddhists reject these practices to distinguish Buddhist marriage from Hindu marriage and to assert a break from caste-bound ritual traditions. This rejection is politically significant. Yet an important question remains. Does removing these symbols transform the gendered structure of marriage?

Too often, reform takes the form of substitution rather than transformation. In many Hindu weddings, brides wear red sarees, red bangles, and marital ornaments. In some Ambedkarite weddings, these are replaced with white sarees, white bangles, and other Buddhist symbols. The colour changes. The religious reference changes. Yet marriage continues to be written onto the female body. The issue, therefore, is not whether women wear red or white. The deeper question is why women remain the primary bearers of marriage, community identity, and moral respectability. Dalit women have long been expected to uphold community honour and, increasingly, to visibly embody anti-caste reform through marriage rituals. Under Brahmanical patriarchy, women’s bodies became sites through which caste was reproduced. Within some anti-caste spaces, they continue to function as the primary sites through which reform is displayed.

When Ambedkarite communities reject sindur and the mangalsutra , do they free women from ritual marking, or do they assign women new forms of symbolic labour? If women are still expected to visibly embody marriage while men remain largely unmarked, then the gendered structure of marriage has not fundamentally changed. It has simply acquired a new political language. This is not an argument against Buddhist weddings or against rejecting Brahmanical symbols. Such refusals remain politically meaningful. The challenge is to move beyond symbolic substitution. Why should marriage be visibly marked on women’s bodies at all? Why is reform measured through women’s appearance rather than through transforming gendered relations? If anti-caste politics seeks the annihilation of caste, then marriage reform must also challenge the gendered division of symbolic labour. Women should participate in marriage as equal subjects, not as carriers of community identity or political transformation.

This critique also turns inward. A Dalit women Ambedkarite perspective does not question only Brahmanical traditions. It also asks anti-caste communities to examine how gendered expectations travel into spaces of reform. Liberation requires more than replacing symbols. It requires reimagining rituals, relationships, and marriage itself so that women are no longer expected to visibly embody reform. Instead, anti-caste transformation should be realised through transformed social relations rather than through the regulation of women’s bodies.

Ambedkarite Marriage: Between Collective Uplift and Status Matching

A deeper contradiction appears in contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices. Ambedkarite ethics call for transforming social relations, including marriage. Yet partner selection often follows status matching. People may express a willingness to marry across marginalised Dalit sub-castes, but these positions often change over time. Many begin to seek partners who are more educated, socially respected, economically secure, or from higher-status backgrounds. Marriage thus becomes not a means of collective transformation but a strategy of individual mobility.

This shift is visible in everyday conversations. Some middle-class Dalit women seek highly educated or high-status Dalit men, or upper-caste men. Some educated Dalit men aspire to marry upper-caste women or middle-class Dalit women. In such cases, aspirations for upward mobility outweigh commitments to anti-caste solidarity. If everyone seeks to marry upward, where do the most marginalised go? When marriage becomes organised around education, class, and social status, those with fewer resources and greater social stigma face increasing exclusion. A process of social closure emerges. Marriage opportunities become concentrated among those who already possess educational, cultural, and economic advantages. The most marginalised, particularly women from poorer families and historically marginalised Dalit sub-castes, bear the greatest cost.

Even Ambedkarite marriage can therefore become a site of status reproduction. Preferences for status matching reproduce inequalities within Dalit communities and reflect what Ambedkar (1936) described as graded inequality. Hierarchy does not remain outside the community. It becomes internalised and shapes intimate decisions. Ideas of compatibility, respectability, and personal choice often conceal deeper assumptions about worth, status, and social mobility.

This pattern also raises important questions about the meaning of collective uplift. Ambedkarite politics has long emphasised the advancement of the community as a whole. If marriage primarily benefits those who already possess educational, cultural, and economic advantages, the ethical principle of lifting one another loses its force. Marriage becomes a mechanism through which inequality is reproduced rather than reduced.

Supporters of these patterns often invoke the language of inter-caste marriage, love marriage, and individual choice. Such marriages undoubtedly challenge important caste boundaries and often involve considerable social risk. Yet the question is not simply whether a marriage crosses caste boundaries. It is also which inter-caste marriages become desirable and celebrated. If they primarily facilitate upward social, educational, or economic mobility, then the language of choice may obscure continuing inequalities within marriage networks. The issue, therefore, is not whether inter-caste or love marriages are progressive. The deeper question is whether they advance the Ambedkarite ideal of collective uplift. If opportunities continue to concentrate among those who already possess social, cultural, and economic advantages, marriage will reproduce new forms of inequality within an anti-caste framework. The challenge is to examine not only the crossing of caste boundaries but also the distribution of opportunity, dignity, and recognition within the community itself.

Ambedkarite Marriage and the Political Economy of Contemporary Wedding Display

A further contradiction emerges in contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices. Many Ambedkarites challenge caste hierarchy, Brahmanical patriarchy, and social inequality in public life. Yet marriage often remains a domain where these commitments are only partially realised.

Many Ambedkarite weddings continue to resemble upper-caste models of celebration. Displays of gold, elaborate decorations, professional photography, multiple ceremonies, and expensive wedding attire have become increasingly common. Within the community, such weddings are sometimes jokingly compared to the lavish celebrations of the Ambani family. Behind the humour lies a broader sociological pattern. Weddings increasingly function as arenas of competitive status display. Brahmanical ritual symbols may disappear, yet prestige and distinction remain central to the celebration. If Ambedkarite weddings continue to reproduce upper-caste ideals of status and display, in what sense do they represent a different model of marriage? The issue is especially significant for poorer and more marginalised families. Rising wedding expenditure creates standards that many cannot realistically meet. Those with greater economic resources gain visibility and prestige, while those with fewer resources face increasing exclusion. Such practices resemble what Veblen (1899) described as conspicuous consumption and what Bourdieu (1977) analysed as distinction. Weddings become occasions for displaying economic success as much as celebrating marriage. What appears as celebration can also reproduce inequality within the community.

The challenge facing Ambedkarite communities therefore extends beyond removing Brahmanical rituals. It requires transforming the social values that organise marriage itself. Ambedkar (1936) described caste as a system of graded inequality in which each group seeks relative superiority. That logic can survive conversion, education, and political consciousness through everyday aspirations and status practices. The question, therefore, is not simply whether a wedding appears Hindu or Buddhist. It is whether marriage strengthens collective solidarity and mutual uplift or reproduces new forms of hierarchy within the community.

The Absence of a Standard Buddhist Marriage Model

There is no universally standardised  Buddhist marriage model within the Ambedkarite tradition. Following the mass conversion movement of 1956, Ambedkarite marriages can be developed through diverse regional and community practices rather than a fixed ritual code. Ambedkar did not seek to prescribe every aspect of marriage. In a letter to V. S. Kardak dated 4 December 1956, he outlined a simple Buddhist marriage ceremony. He rejected homa and saptapadi and prescribed an earthen pot, a shared cotton thread, the recitation of the Mangala Sutta , and white clothing for both bride and groom. His support for legal and civil marriage also pointed towards separating marriage from Brahmanical ritual authority.

Ambedkar’s letter should be read as a proposal for a simple Buddhist marriage ceremony rather than a comprehensive blueprint for Buddhist marriage. It offered practical guidance while leaving future generations to reinterpret marriage in light of Ambedkarite ethics and changing social realities. This question becomes particularly significant in rural Dalit communities, where marriage is experienced not simply as a legal union but as a collective social institution that creates kinship, reciprocity, community recognition, and belonging. The challenge, therefore, is to develop forms of marriage that embody anti-caste ethics while remaining meaningful in different social contexts.

Contemporary Ambedkarite weddings therefore combine Buddhist recitations with locally familiar customs. These hybrid forms reflect continuing efforts to reinterpret marriage within an Ambedkarite ethical framework. Debates surrounding “mixed marriages” illustrate this ongoing process. Some inherited Hindu practices are criticised, while others remain largely unquestioned. Rather than representing a fixed ritual tradition, Ambedkarite marriage remains an evolving social project shaped through reflection, debate, and collective experimentation.

Debates over “mixed marriages” and the continued practice of the baraat reveal important tensions within contemporary Ambedkarite marriage practices in Odisha. Many Ambedkarites reject Brahmanical rituals such as Sanskrit mantras, Brahmin priests, sindur , and the mangalsutra . Yet practices such as the baraat , status matching through social closure, and competitive wedding expenditure often remain largely unquestioned. These practices reproduce masculine prestige, social distinction, and new forms of inequality within the community. They also narrow marriage opportunities for the most marginalised, particularly women, challenging the Ambedkarite commitment to collective uplift.

This paper has argued that the question is not simply whether a marriage appears Hindu or Buddhist. The deeper question is whether marriage transforms the social relations through which caste, patriarchy, status, and inequality are reproduced. Ambedkarite marriage should therefore be understood not as a completed ritual tradition but as an unfinished social and ethical project. Its transformative potential depends on the willingness of Ambedkarite communities to critically examine inherited practices and to imagine new forms of marriage that embody equality, dignity, and collective responsibility.

title: Media community faces killings, weaponization of laws under Marcos Jr.
content:
A placard highlighting a call to stop the attacks against community journalists placed on the floor during a protest action at the UP College of Media and Communication on May 2, 2025, a day before World Press Freedom Day. Photo by Alex Culla/Bulatlat

“Protecting press freedom is a shared responsibility. Without it, the public’s right to know and the foundations of democratic society are at risk.”

CAGAYAN DE ORO — Four years since Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assumed the presidency, press freedom violations continue.

Eleven journalists and media workers were killed under his administration, according to the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP), although two of them were initially reported as not work-related. The latest case happened in May when Nestor Micator , radio broadcaster of D’Empire Radio, was shot dead by an unidentified assailant in Malidegao town which is under the Special Geographic Area of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

Community journalist RJ Nichole Ledesma was also killed during a military operation in Toboso, Negros Occidental, in April. He was reportedly in the area doing community work. However, the Philippine Army stressed that he was a New People’s Army (NPA) combatant, a claim assailed by media and human rights organizations.

Roxas City-based broadcaster Jay Lavapiez , meanwhile, encountered a near-death experience after he was ambushed in June.

In May, the Presidential Task Force on Media Security (PTFoMS) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) for what they called stronger collaboration and case buildup efforts.

PTFoMS also signed a MOA with the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) last year. Aside from advocating to expedite the resolution of cases, the agreement would establish a rapid response mechanism, psychosocial assistance for victims, and capacity-building and prevention for media workers.

The Philippine National Police (PNP), in partnership with PTFoMS and other government agencies, launched the PNP Media Security Vanguards program aimed at enhancing the safety and security of media practitioners.

Read: Media groups decry harassment of journalists, activist during protest

The NUJP, however, stressed that the State has failed to bring to justice the masterminds behind these killings. Among them were the murders of Renato Blanco, Percival Mabasa , Cresenciano Bundoquin , Juan Jumalon, Juan Dayang , Erwin Segovia , Noel Samar , and Julito Calo . “While four suspects behind two of these killings have been arrested, no mastermind has been brought to justice,” NUJP said in an earlier statement.

Read: Philippines remains dangerous for journalists

The group backed the proposal of Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and Opinion Irene Khan for the Philippine government to establish a “Special Prosecutor” for crimes against journalists and human rights defenders.

On the other hand, the local press freedom group also monitored the filing of cases against journalists and media workers. Aside from libel and cyberlibel, the Data Privacy Act and unjust vexation were reportedly weaponized as a usual form of retaliation against the media community.

Bacolod-based journalist Marchel Espina surrendered to the authorities upon learning that there was an arrest warrant issued against her for an unjust vexation case which stemmed from an opinion piece published in SunStar Cebu in 2024 when she was still the editor-in-chief.

The same charges were filed against Negros Occidental-based journalist Erwin Delilan in the first quarter of 2026 after the complainants got annoyed with his Binalaybay —a term used for Hiligaynon poems—commentaries on social media. Delilan was arrested twice prior to posting bail.

Lavapiez and his wife, India , who is also a radio broadcaster, also faced multiple cyberlibel cases filed by local officials. In August 2025, the Sangguniang Bayan of Sigma declared the two personas non grata for allegedly disseminating false and misleading information.

Cases of alleged violation of the Data Privacy Act were also filed against the late DZRH reporter Misael Gonzales Jr. after publishing the details indicated in an arrest warrant, as well as iFM Cagayan de Oro News Director Menzie Montes for posting screenshots of her conversation with a local official.

The NUJP monitored 15 libel and cyberlibel cases and 17 other forms of judicial harassment so far. These formed part of the overall 250 press freedom violations under the Marcos Jr. administration.

Tacloban-based journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio has been in detention since February 2020 because of trumped-up criminal charges. While she got acquitted on other charges, she was convicted for allegedly financing terrorism. Her conviction is being appealed.

NUJP pointed out the possible effects when journalists are slapped with cases. Aside from financial burden and psychological trauma, it reiterated that it has a chilling effect which could lead to self-censorship and content takedown, to name a few.

In a forum organized by NUJP and the De La Salle University-Department of Communication on July 25, lawyer Gilbert Andres, executive director of the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) Philippines, underscored the importance for journalists and media workers of knowing the available and appropriate legal remedies.

He said that journalists and media workers could also take legal attacks by filing complaints for damages against those who filed cases against them.

In its State of Media Freedom report released in this year’s World Press Freedom Day, the media watchdog Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR) urged the Philippine government to revisit laws that may be used against journalists.

“Protecting press freedom is a shared responsibility. Without it, the public’s right to know and the foundations of democratic society are at risk,” CMFR said in its report. (DAA)

Disclosure: Bulatlat editor-in-chief Ronalyn Olea is the secretary-general of the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines.
