title: Recognized, but not prioritized? LGBTQIA+ rights absent from past Marcos SONAs
content:
Kath Rabang working on an art project. Photo courtesy of Kath Rabang.

“Recognition is not enough without concrete rights.”

By Kasheena Camacho Bulatlat.com

Related story: We all deserve to bask in sunshine

MANILA — Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has publicly recognized the LGBTQIA+ community through Executive Order No. 51, annual Pride Month statements, and meetings with LGBTQIA+ organizations since taking office in 2022. But a review of his four State of the Nation Addresses (SONA) found no explicit mention of LGBTQIA+ rights, the proposed Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression, and Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC) Equality Bill, or other national legislative measures protecting LGBTQIA+ Filipinos.

The absence of LGBTQIA+ rights from four consecutive SONAs comes despite executive initiatives recognizing the community and years-long calls from advocates to enact a national anti-discrimination legislation.

For some LGBTQIA+ Filipinos, the gap between public recognition and legal protection is reflected not in policy documents but in their everyday interactions with schools, workplaces, hospitals, and even their own families.

For Cleothena (not her real name), a transgender woman employed at a government agency who requested anonymity for fear of workplace repercussions, that gap became apparent only weeks after she started working.

“When I first entered the organization, they asked me how I wanted to be addressed. I thought they respected who I was,” she said.

Several weeks later, a security guard informed her that she could no longer use the women’s restroom after the human resources office reportedly received complaints from other employees.

“They told me there had been complaints. I asked them, ‘Where am I supposed to use the restroom now?’ They gave me only two options—the men’s restroom or the restroom for persons with disabilities. No policy was ever shown to me. We were simply told that I was no longer allowed to use the women’s restroom.”

During Pride Month, the agency temporarily designated the PWD restroom as an all-gender restroom, she said.

“After June, they removed the sign. Then they told me to use the men’s restroom again.”

Fearing the decision could affect her employment, she chose not to pursue a formal complaint and instead began using restrooms in another building.

“I felt like I had to hide. As long as no one was watching, I could quietly use the restroom. As long as no one confronts me,” she said.

Cleothena’s experience is one of many that LGBTQIA+ advocates say illustrate the gap between symbolic recognition and meaningful legal protection.

Bahaghari Spokesperson Yell Teresa said the Marcos administration’s public recognition of the LGBTQIA+ community has yet to translate into substantive legal protections.

“More than three years after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assumed office, the promise of an inclusive and just society for the LGBTQIA+ sector remains hollow,” Teresa said in a written response to Bulatlat. “Recognition is not enough without concrete rights.”

Cleothena’s experience is not unique.

Kath Rabang, a lesbian, said she also encountered discrimination in school and in her personal life because of her sexual orientation.

At her former Catholic school, Rabang said she was required to wear the prescribed girls’ uniform despite asking to wear pants.

“During that time, it was a no-brainer situation because despite my appeal, I wasn’t allowed to wear pants,” she said.

Outside school, Rabang said discrimination also affected her relationship with her former partner.

She recalled that her partner’s mother discovered they were in a relationship before they were ready to come out, forcing them to hide from relatives and acquaintances.

“We had to be careful every time we met because we were afraid someone who knew her family might see us,” she said.

Although Rabang believes acceptance of LGBTQIA+ Filipinos has improved over the years, she said meaningful support should extend beyond public statements.

“It gives me hope because it shows that our experiences are being acknowledged. But support should go beyond words and lead to real action that protects LGBTQIA+ people from discrimination,” she said.

She said stronger anti-discrimination laws, accessible support systems, and legal recognition of LGBTQIA+ couples in matters such as hospital decision-making would better reflect government support.

Student organizations said that similar concerns continue to surface on university campuses.

At the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Kasarianlan said the organization regularly receives reports involving discrimination against LGBTQIA+ students, with deadnaming and restrictions on restroom access among the most common concerns.

“The most common form of discrimination we continue to encounter is deadnaming,” said Rianne Dacanay, President of Kasarianlan. “We also receive reports from transgender students who are prevented from using restrooms that correspond with their gender identity.”

Although the organization does not maintain a formal database, Dacanay said Kasarianlan receives fewer than 10 reports per month, most of which involve incidents within the university. Students are referred to the university’s Gender Office or the Committee on Decorum and Investigation (CODI), which handles complaints involving gender-based violations.

The Commission on Higher Education (Ched), meanwhile, said it could not provide records of complaints involving LGBTQIA+ students because such cases form part of confidential administrative proceedings protected under the Data Privacy Act.

Instead, Ched pointed to institutional compliance with existing policies. According to the commission, 80.7 percent of responding higher education institutions have established a Committee on Decorum and Investigation (CODI), 92.1 percent have adopted a Code of Conduct, and 89.4 percent have incorporated the code into their student handbooks, in line with the implementation of the Safe Spaces Act and CHED Memorandum Order No. 3, series of 2022.

While institutional mechanisms exist, advocates say they do not replace comprehensive national legal protections against discrimination.

The experiences of Cleothena, Rabang, and LGBTQIA+ students reflect what advocates say is the consequence of the absence of comprehensive national legal protections.

While discrimination continues to surface in workplaces, schools, and other institutions, the Marcos administration has taken several executive steps recognizing the LGBTQIA+ community.

In June 2023, Malacañang said it “honors the impact of the LGBTQIA+ community” in celebration of Pride Month. Marcos Jr has also met with LGBTQIA+ organizations and, in June 2025, he signed Executive Order No. 51 creating the Special Committee on LGBTQIA+ Affairs.

Executive Order No. 51 created an interagency body tasked with coordinating government programs and policies concerning LGBTQIA+ Filipinos. However, the order does not establish enforceable legal rights or prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or sex characteristics.

Those protections remain the objective of the long-pending SOGIESC Equality Bill, which seeks to prohibit discrimination in employment, education, healthcare, housing, and access to public services.

For Bahaghari, the omission of LGBTQIA+ concerns from four consecutive SONAs carries policy implications because the annual address outlines the administration’s legislative priorities.

“The SONA serves as the direction of the government’s national policies and priorities. When LGBTQIA+ issues continue to be left out, it sends the message that these are not considered urgent concerns that the state must address,” Teresa said.

Bahaghari urged the administration to move beyond symbolic recognition by prioritizing the passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill and strengthening protections against discrimination across public institutions.

For Rabang, official recognition of the LGBTQIA+ community offers hope, but it cannot replace legal protection.

“It gives me hope because it shows that our experiences are being acknowledged,” she said. “But support should go beyond words and lead to real action that protects LGBTQIA+ people from discrimination.”

She said meaningful government support would include stronger anti-discrimination laws, accessible support systems for LGBTQIA+ people facing abuse or rejection, and legal recognition of same-sex couples in matters such as hospital decision-making.

Student leaders shared the same call.

Dacanay said Kasarianlan welcomes gestures recognizing the LGBTQIA+ community but believes these should be accompanied by concrete legislative action, particularly the passage of the long-pending SOGIESC Equality Bill.

“I really hope in the upcoming SONA, President Marcos could at least mention something to really pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill,” Dacanay said. “If he could at least mention it, it would give the House a wake-up call to really move the bill.”

Bahaghari likewise urged the administration to move beyond symbolic recognition by making LGBTQIA+ rights part of its legislative agenda.

“The fight for LGBTQIA+ rights is inseparable from the broader struggle for human rights and social justice,” Teresa said. “As long as people continue to be denied dignity and equal treatment because of their sexual orientation or gender identity, our society cannot truly be considered free and just.”

Watch: The LGBTQIA+ community in the Philippines remains vulnerable to discrimination and hate crimes

For Cleothena, however, the issue extends beyond policies and public statements. It is about being able to live and work without fear of discrimination.

“Anyone can say they support us,” she said. “But support means action.”

She said she hopes the government will finally enact measures that provide meaningful legal protection for LGBTQIA+ Filipinos, beginning with the passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill.

“I hope the SOGIESC Equality Bill will finally be passed. We have rights, too, as human beings. I hope there will come a time when we can live normal lives without having to worry about discrimination or about someone stepping on our dignity.” (AMU, RVO)

title: As Senegal Cracks Down on LGBTQ Rights, Activists Seek Help From Abroad
content:
“I prefer to remain anonymous because of the authorities in Senegal,” Mamadou, one of the founders of the Senegalese LGBTQ rights organization Free Senegal, told Unicorn Riot. Speaking under an alias, Mamadou agreed to speak with Unicorn Riot only if he could remain anonymous. He fled the country in 2021 after years of harassment and is one of many now worried for their safety amid a wave of anti-LGBTQ repression that took hold this year.




His fears are not unfounded. Since February, Senegalese authorities have initiated a crackdown against the LGBTQ community, reportedly arresting hundreds across the country. Local newspapers announce new arrests every week, including of celebrities.




The recent crackdown started after the dismantling of a suspected French-Senegalese pedophilia ring in early February. It culminated with Parliament passing a new anti-LGBTQ law by an overwhelming majority in March, which doubled prison sentences for “acts against nature” to up to 10 years.




Under this provision, the law equates same-sex relationships with sexual crimes such as bestiality and necrophilia. Furthermore, in a separate article, it stipulates a sentence of up to seven years in prison for the “promotion or financing” of homosexuality, bisexuality, or transgender identity.




According to Free Senegal, at least 184 members of the LGBTQ community have been detained and jailed as of early April. “Those who are not detained are trying to flee the country because they are afraid for their security. There is a mass exodus,” said Mamadou.




“All community leaders have left, members of organizations have left. There are currently no allies of the community in Senegal,” he added.




Mamadou describes an atmosphere of panic where LGBTQ individuals are being arrested after being reported to the police, often by those close to them or identified after authorities search the phones of detainees. Even lawyers are hesitant to take their cases for fear of being targeted themselves. 




Due to this restrictive environment, LGBTQ individuals in Senegal have to turn to either informal support networks or organizations outside Senegal for help. One of them is the Canadian LGBTQ rights organization Rainbow Railroad, which provides assistance to persecuted LGBTQ individuals around the world.




According to Chief Programs Officer Devon Matthews, the organization, until early April had already received 90 requests for help from Senegalese citizens, a sharp increase compared to 2025, when it received 106 the whole year. The number of requests followed domestic developments, with a spike in early March during the discussion and voting on the law.




The organization does not have an on-the-ground presence in Senegal, however, it is drawing from its experience in 

Uganda

 and other African countries to assist the community in the country.




Uganda’s Death Sentence on its LGBTI+ Communities

 [2023]




“We’re trying to focus most of our efforts right now internally on the activists and organizations that we are aware of, some of whom are reaching out to us directly,” said Matthews, adding that Rainbow Railroad is providing limited financial assistance, helping connect activists with one another and offering support with information and logistics.




“Right after these laws are passed, certain activists are [being] targeted or [put] on government lists. What we want to do is just make sure that those activists are able to either temporarily leave or move from the city to a quieter area while the dust from the law settles,” she said. “That’s the first request that we often get.”




Matthews adds that although Rainbow Railroad is able to refer 250 LGBTQ refugees each year directly to the Canadian government for resettlement in Canada, the program is reserved only for the most vulnerable of individuals who have already fled to a third country and the process takes years.




While Senegalese activists are trying to avoid arrest and persecution, those who campaigned in favor of the anti-LGBTQ law have allies in the highest echelons of the parliamentary majority party, PASTEF. Its leader, Senegal’s former prime minister, Ousmane Sonko, pledged to impose tougher penalties for homosexuality during the 2024 election campaign.




“We were received by the president of the National Assembly and by the head of the majority parliamentary group PASTEF,” said Sokhna Ndeye Diop, the president of the women’s wing of the powerful association of Islamist organizations called And Samm Jikko Yi, during an interview with Unicorn Riot. Diop is also the wife of a PASTEF MP.




For years, And Samm Jikko Yi, which in Wolof translates to “Together for the Preservation of Values,” has organized rallies and campaigned for stricter legislation against homosexuality. In 2021, along with several MPs, they proposed a draft law that largely formed the basis of the current legislation.




There have been reports that during that campaign, And Samm Jikko Yi worked with the American anti-LGBTQ group 

MassResistance

. However, Diop denies this, saying that the Sengalese organization’s former coordinator contacted MassResistance in a personal capacity, without the knowledge of the rest of the organization.




“The Senegalese people, unanimously, do not accept homosexuality. Even when you try to bury a homosexual in a cemetery, people say ‘no,’” she said, referring to an incident in 2023 in the city of Kaolack where a crowd exhumed the body of a man accused of being gay and paraded it through the streets before burning it in the city’s square.




While such incidents are rare, public opinion in the country toward same-sex relationships and LGBTQ rights remains overwhelmingly negative. In a July 2025 survey by 

Afrobarometer

, 97% of Senegalese respondents said they would not want a “homosexual person as a neighbor,” a figure virtually unchanged since 2014.




Although Mamadou is not optimistic about the future he says he will continue advocating for LGBTQ rights in Senegal. “We are in France for security reasons, but we have not forgotten why we are here. The struggle we led back home is what matters most and it is that struggle we continue here.”

title: New Book Examines Women and Queer People Convicted for Crimes That Never Occurred
content:
According to the 

National Registry of Exonerations

, roughly three-quarters of women exonerated after wrongful convictions involve cases where no crime actually occurred—the wrongfully convicted women faced charges for acts of self-defense, stillbirths and miscarriages, or accidental deaths.




Valena Beety’s new book, 

Pink Crime: Fighting Against the Criminalization of Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Queer Identity

, examines the connections between junk science and gender bias that fuels these wrongful convictions—a category of cases she calls “Pink Crime.” 




“These are criminal cases that are about punishing women and queer people for their bodily autonomy, for their gender, for their gender performance,” Beety told The Appeal. “The criminal legal system is being used to silence people, surveil, punish, and truly erase people who don’t conform.”




Proving innocence in these cases is a particularly Herculean task, says Beety, who has litigated many innocence cases herself and is co-founder of the Indiana Innocence Project. 




“DNA evidence is very helpful in reversing a conviction because it’s showing it’s not one person who did it, it’s another person,” Beety says. 




But if there was no crime, “there was no perpetrator.”




“It requires a completely different framework,” Beety says of no-crime wrongful convictions. “If you have prosecutors and courts in post-conviction that are dead set on, ‘Well, the only way a conviction is reversed is if you have DNA evidence,’ then that misses the majority of women who are in prison and have been wrongly convicted.”




Below is our interview with Beety about 

Pink Crime

. The interview has been edited for clarity. 













The Appeal in Your Inbox




Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.






















Sign Up
















The Appeal

: You write, “Protecting the innocent and exemplary person does not shrink the carceral state; it only fortifies it.” Could you elaborate on what that means?




Valena Beety

: This goes back to the idea of the perfect victim, which has worked against women and queer people for decades. You have survivors of domestic violence who fought back against their attacker, and they instead are the ones who are criminalized. Or you survive domestic violence or sexual violence, and you’re a sex worker, and you’re criminalized because of that. Or you call the police from your home, and your children are there, and the police come, and you’re charged with child neglect for failing to protect your children from your abusive partner. This is all tied to a perfect victim, a perfect survivor. To be that perfect victim as a woman, as a queer person, it’s about performing gender and performing gender well enough to be sympathetic—that you are worthy of help instead of punishment. 




The Appeal

: You write about how junk science intersects with pink crime. Can you define junk science? Can you talk about how it intersects with the topic of your book—the criminalization of queer identity, motherhood, and pregnancy?




VB

: Junk science is a label that is often applied to forensic evidence. Forensic evidence is evidence from forensic disciplines that came up in police investigations. These were types of evidence that were created by the police for the purpose of being able to identify a suspect as the perpetrator and convict them so they’re biased from the very beginning. 




When we’re thinking about this, we’re thinking about shoeprints, we’re thinking about fingerprints, we’re thinking about bite marks, we’re thinking about fire science investigations. These all grew up in police investigations. That’s where they came from. They did not come from a scientific lab where you have a hypothesis and the hypothesis is tested for whether it is accurate, for whether it is reliable. 




The only forensic evidence that is truly scientific evidence is DNA, and that did grow up in a lab, with hypothesis testing for its reliability and accuracy. DNA evidence has been able to prove these forensic disciplines are faulty. 




Forensic evidence wasn’t about finding out if the evidence was reliable on its own. It was instead about creating evidence to convict defendants. We’re seeing this being used today in real time in these charges based on pregnancy, based on parenting, and based on queer identity. 




We see prosecutors who are trying to bring charges of murder against people who have a stillbirth, and what they use is the floating lung test. This is a test literally from when we would accuse women of being witches and throw them in the river, and if they drowned, they were innocent, but if they floated, they were guilty, and then they would be murdered by the state. This is how old this test is and it is incredibly unreliable.




You take a piece of lung from the fetus and you put it in water to see if it floats. The idea is that if the piece of lung floats, then the baby was born and took its first breath. This test is not only notoriously unreliable, it also gives false positives. 




The last example I’ll give is drug tests and drug testing people who are giving birth in a hospital. These drug tests are not necessarily reliable, and they also don’t indicate [that] there’s any harm to a child. A lot of these fetal harm charges are brought when there’s a positive drug test even when there is a healthy baby.




Giving birth to a healthy child is not necessarily going to be enough to protect someone who is pregnant from allegations that they’ve caused some fetal harm. But having a child who does have health conditions at birth, immediately healthcare providers, with social workers, with police, turn on the pregnant person and say, “What did you do to cause this? What behaviors did you do or not do?” And this is so expansive. This can be: “Were you walking enough? Did you get enough bed rest? What were you eating? Did you eat soft cheeses? Did you eat certain kinds of fish?”




The Appeal

: You write about how the majority of known wrongful convictions of women involve cases where no crime occurred. Is there any understanding of why that is? 




VB

: According to the National Registry of Exonerations, up to 75 percent of women who were wrongly convicted in the United States were wrongly convicted where no crime occurred. 




So what does that mean? That means there was no criminal act. [For example] there was a space heater that started a fire and yet police thought that the woman was at the home and intentionally set the fire. Police and prosecutors rely on faulty forensic evidence, fire science evidence, and they combine that with gender stereotypes. This is a bad mother, a bad wife, a bad woman who intentionally set the fire. The woman is wrongly convicted based on that confluence of falsehood forensic evidence and gender bias. 




The Appeal

: What inspired you to write this book? 




VB

: I am a queer woman. I’m married to another woman, and we have a child. We’re a queer family. We were moving back to my home state of Indiana when we were pregnant. Indiana had made abortion illegal in all but the most extreme circumstances, and we knew that there might be pregnancy difficulties, and if there were, we would not have access to abortion. If there were pregnancy difficulties, we could be blamed for that. 




Being queer parents, we are, just by our identities, looked at as more likely to be dangerous towards children. We have never taken bathtub photos of our child because we know that there’s a different lens that can be applied to us as queer people, and it’s a criminalizing lens. That’s what really motivated me to connect the dots to create this term, pink crime, to say, “Hey, this is all going back to gender bias and people in power using the criminal legal system as a lever to punish women and queer people who don’t conform to gender norms.” 




In my home state of Indiana, 

our governor proclaimed

 June to be officially “Nuclear Family Month,” which is a man and a woman married with biological children. Our lieutenant governor even posted, “Take back the rainbow.” 




[In their minds] there’s only one model for how people can be a family, and otherwise, you are deviant. This all plays a role in not only why I wrote the book, but why I continue to talk about it and continue to care about it.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Reflections on a decade of UK Black Lives Matter
content:
From Freedom News (09/08/2026)

This racist violence we experience is an active race?making project serving the interests of capital

Black Lives Matter UK was founded by activists who had worked together on previous deaths in police custody, both in the US and Britain.

In the US, it had started as a love letter to Black people in the aftermath of George Zimmerman’s acquittal – who killed 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012 for the crime of carrying Skittles while Black in a gated community.

In Britain our martyr was Mark Duggan, killed by the Met in 2011. We not only remember the anti-Black propaganda about his criminality, how even some radical leftists argued he needed to die, how the army needed to be brought in to control rioters. We remember the public disregard of his and Black life in general. We live with the reality of State harassment and violence in terms of stop and search, legal sexual assault in terms of strip searches. State racist violence is not only structural, it structures the British economy and State legitimacy.

Today, which is worse than in 2011, almost one in two Black children do not get three meals a day. Ethnically Black African children do better than white British children in GCSEs, but are less likely to get a paid job. All of this motivates us because it is our lived reality.

“I can’t breathe” was said 11 times by Eric Garner, a father of four, who was strangled to death, on camera, by a New York cop in 2014. His death sparked the second iteration of Black Lives Matter protests across the US, and in Britain that became the 2014 Westfield protest.

Sean Rigg, who died in police custody at Brixton Station in 2008, Roger Sylvester in Tottenham in 1999. Jimmy Mubenga in 2010. Those names were with us as we decided to form Black Lives Matter UK.

The US has always been used as a way to paint Britain as moderate, because “we’re not like America.” British policing is seen as sensible. We don’t have guns.

So part of the struggle was not only to continue the fight for accountability, but also about how to make these struggles more visible. How do we honour the lives that have been lost, which continue to be discarded by the State? The thing about Mark Duggan’s death wasn’t just that the police were seen as heroic, they were seen as doing what needed to be done. What that says is when you are stopped and searched, or your home is raided on spurious grounds, when children are asked to be undressed in front of police officials, this is for the public good. You deserve this.

And we wanted a politics of refusal.

We came from different traditions. We weren’t all from one Trotskyist group, some were more liberal, I’m from a more anarchist strand. These tensions played out in asking who do we appeal to? In 2016, all of us came to a conclusion on the day after the Brexit referendum, when we saw on the front page of The Sun newspaper, actual neo-Nazis wearing Vote Leave T-shirts celebrating their victory. For us that was indicative of what was to come. A new revived form of White supremacy. Ten years on, you can judge for yourselves if that’s accurate.

So we agreed to protest on the fifth anniversary of the police killing of Mark Duggan. On Friday August 5th 2016, to the soundtrack of Skepta’s Shutdown, we were going to shut down Heathrow Airport, Birmingham Airport, Nottingham Central. With the motivation of Brexit and police State violence. The impunity with which the police could kill and be told it’s good.

We did disrupt these things. We had people ready to go to the media to explain Britain is not innocent. That Britain’s imperial legacy is framed to perpetuate its present, where Black people are systematically discriminated against. Not only in the criminal punishment system but in education, employment, housing, health outcomes. Every facet of life.

The liberal arguments that we normally hear are around unconscious bias, unintended consequences, the lag of the State to modernise in a multi-racial democracy and as a result, that policies designed to benefit all people have a disproportionate effect on minoritised groups who live mostly in deprived areas – i.e. State violence towards the working class is normal, it just happens to particularly affect Black and Asian people.

We reject this. While it is true that Black and Asian people live in more deprived areas. It’s not happenstance. The way the economy is structured means there are people classified as disposable. This is how the global economy works. The capitalist economy demands child slaves in DR Congo to dig radioactive coltan with their bare hands, which is then used to power our mobile phones. That violence is absolutely normal.

And the global imperial white supremacist perspective is also how Britain governs internal populations, “naturally”, according to that logic.

But it is not just the outflow of racial capitalism into Britain, these are active decisions by policy makers to remake race, and racism, in new forms. We see this in the Prevent program. A lot of Black people are Muslim, and the racialising logic of Prevent trains NHS workers, teachers, social workers etc. to see racialised Muslims as a threat. Which means six-year-old Muslim kids in the north of England misspell the word “cucumber”, and it’s read as “cook bomb”.

This racist violence we experience and tolerate is not a legacy of the past or unintended consequence. It is an active race-making project serving the interests of capital, but more broadly It offers a psychic wage. It’s a way of buying off the white working class with small benefits.

Today BLM UK is made up of radical leftists from social democrats to Black anarchists. We do not have very strong political lines, other than that we organise towards Black liberation. And that we believe Black liberation is bound up with that of the working class as a whole. We don’t think you can create a Black, liberated island in a sea of white supremacy, or a world of racial capitalism. These things go together, and have to be destroyed together. But we believe Black autonomy is crucial.

So, that sets the stage of how we’ve operated and organised.

In 2020, unexpectedly, BLM UK raised £1.2 million through a crowdfunder. We had no expectation we would be anywhere near that – previously we’d raised about £8,000. It was raised by 36,000 small donations, primarily individuals and small groups.

When we received it, we decided that it wasn’t ours. That we had, surprisingly, been entrusted with this large amount of money, and we needed to actually redistribute 50% to organisations that were fighting oppression, racism, and so on. We funded organisations that had a large Black presence, but weren’t always Black-led, like the UVW and IWGB unions. We actually also funded organisations that were Black-led, and we thought that was where the majority of the funds should go, like the United Families and Friends Coalition Against Deaths in Custody (UFFC), who we worked with at the Westfield shutdown.

So we’ve redistributed more than half a million pounds to lots of groups that were working towards Black liberation in a multitude of ways, not just trade unions, but domestic violence support, groups that actually were just organising Black people to ramble in the countryside without fear of racist harassment.

Once we’d redistributed half of the money, the second task was that we not only needed to redistribute funds, we needed to create an organisation that would actually defend Black people.

We were mindful that there wasn’t an organisation with the single focus of Black liberation. And we thought it was incumbent on us to try. Not to be the sole repository of that struggle, but to work with communities in a non-hierarchical way.

So BLM started to be an organisation that was more focused on building power. Not State power, but class power – to regularly disrupt the flow of capital. Power to not only force concessions, but build a greater form of full autonomy and build up people’s ability to develop liberation wherever we are. And again, seeing that as being linked with the liberation for our class more generally.

What we’ve done is build campaigns, work with communities from Roma resisting State racism, to the Windrush scandal, which is a form of citizenship stripping, but also, more perniciously, an aspect of the hostile environment. We want to identify that the violence the State reserves for undocumented migrants is not illegitimate because it targets the wrong people, but because the State does not and should not have the right to impose such violence.

We are trying to build up support and allies, but we’re also conducting political education on the State, and the illegitimacy of its violence. We run Project Timbuktu where we are really wanting to understand the nature of the State. Our concern is this pushing or orientating of it towards racist violence. The fear of dawn raids, of people being snatched away. What we’ve seen with ICE raids and confrontations in the US has happened on smaller scales across Britain. Under Reform we will see that renewed, in fact we’ve already seen this under Starmer’s Labour, it has deported more children than any other administration on record. We organise not only to interrupt and disrupt their ability to do that, but to build power to ensure it can never happen again.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Maria da Penha, 20 anos: Alta de feminicídios revela fracasso estatal em proteger mulheres
content:
O Brasil segue sendo um país violento, especialmente para as pessoas negras e para as mulheres. Pelo quarto ano consecutivo, o país registra índices recordes de feminicídios e tentativas de feminicídio, de acordo com o Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública 2026. Apenas no ano passado, foram 1.571 vítimas desse crime, a maioria mulheres negras, assassinadas dentro de casa. A Lei Maria da Penha completa 20 anos, mas a violência contra as mulheres permanece como um dos principais desafios na segurança pública.

Nesta semana, o Pauta Pública recebe Juliana Brandão, advogada e coordenadora de Gênero e Raça do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública. Em entrevista a Andrea Dip, ela analisa os dados do Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública, o impacto do racismo nas taxas de violência, e defende a importância de políticas públicas voltadas à prevenção e ao fortalecimento da rede de proteção às vítimas. “Quando a gente se abstém de pensar em saídas preventivas, a gente está consentindo com essa escalada”, afirma.

Leia os principais pontos da conversa e ouça o podcast completo abaixo.

EP 228 O fracasso do Estado em proteger mulheres – com Juliana Brandão

7 de agosto de 2026 · Coordenadora de gênero e raça do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública analisa as falhas de crimes contra a mulher

Segundo dados do último Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública, em 2025, o Brasil registrou o maior número de feminicídios da série histórica iniciada em 2015, quando a tipificação do crime foi criada no país. De que tipo de violência de gênero estamos falando?

Estamos falando de uma violência que interrompe a vida das mulheres, uma violência que pode ser evitada. Porque o feminicídio, na verdade, é o ápice de um ciclo de violência que se inicia com um empurrão, um tapa, uma humilhação, com a violência psicológica, patrimonial e perseguição. Essas violências acabam sendo naturalizadas e desconsideradas como tal. Com isso, a mulher vai se sentindo cada vez mais enredada nesse ciclo, muitas vezes envergonhada e até se sentindo culpada por estar nessa situação.

Porque estamos falando de uma violência que é cometida por alguém que é do círculo muito próximo dessa mulher. Essa violência do feminicídio, que os dados do anuário trazem agora, é uma violência que acontece na maior parte das vezes dentro de casa, entre quatro paredes. Então, o problema está no ambiente doméstico. O problema está naquilo que acontece quando ninguém vê, quando a porta está fechada.

Quando falamos da violência que atinge também crianças e adolescentes, é também praticada por alguém que é do círculo muito próximo delas e a maior parte das vítimas são meninas negras, que repetem também o perfil das vítimas de feminicídio. Então, temos um endereçamento muito certo dessa violência, que já devia ser um sinal pra gente, um farol para onde a gente tem que olhar se a gente quer de fato mudar essa essa situação que a gente está vivendo.

Houve também um número alto de tentativas de feminicídio. Quer dizer que há falhas na prevenção?

Então, um recrudescimento da violência contra as mulheres, que não se explica tão só por uma melhora de enquadramento penal, mas por uma situação mais geral. title: Trump’s FTC Is Threatening to Punish Big Tech for “Woke AI”
content: To understand the stakes of the debate over AI regulation, look no further than Minnesota, where tech oligarch Elon Musk is once again generating embarrassing headlines. Last week, a federal judge denied a request from Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI to block a Minnesota law banning nude deepfakes used to sexually harass women and girls from taking effect.
